question.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where $a=⟨2,-1,3⟩$ and $b=⟨3,-1,1⟩$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively. If $f(a)=6$ and $f(b)=2,$ then what is missing from the statement below?

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $\text{_______________}\,.$ *
question.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(b)-f(a) & =∇f(c)\cdot (b-a) \\ 2-6 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c),{f}_{z}(c)⟩\cdot (⟨3,-1,1⟩-⟨2,-1,3⟩) \\ -4 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c),{f}_{z}(c)⟩\cdot ⟨1,0,-2⟩ \\ -4 & ={f}_{x}(c)-2{f}_{z}(c).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the complete sentence is as follows:

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that ${f}_{x}(c)-2{f}_{z}(c)=-4.$ *
